source.original_title: 06/01/2026 - Dr Doug Stithem x Ben Byrne KL
source.display_title: 06/01/2026 - Dr Doug Stithem x Ben Byrne KL — Lost

prospect.name: Doug Stithem
prospect.aka: dstithem - the Zoom display name; addressed on the call as Dr. Doug
prospect.occupation: Decompression doctor - owns a spinal decompression practice and sells roughly $10,000, fourteen-month treatment plans to patients with disc problems
prospect.family_status: Married, with a five-year-old son and an eight-year-old daughter. His wife trains with him and both children join in with a five-pound kettlebell.
prospect.training_background: Lifelong weightlifter who kept injuring himself on standard bodybuilding training. For the past eighteen months to two years has trained with kettlebells, macebells and Indian clubs, self-taught from YouTube, and describes himself as 'a YouTube kettlebell warrior'. Reports good results and says his spine feels stronger since switching. Previously used the Ben Patrick (knees-over-toes) programme, submitting video for asynchronous form analysis.
prospect.medical: Injured L5-S1 in a car accident with his wife, resulting in herniations at L5-S1 and L4-L5. Underwent a microdiscectomy, paid roughly $11,000 out of pocket because he holds no health insurance by choice. Says he has since 'fixed them' using his own decompression tables and regular chiropractic adjustment. Reports that high-intensity training in the old bodybuilding style reliably triggered flare-ups, and that kettlebell, macebell and Indian club work has not. Also reports shoulder and back aggravation from heavy lifting. No current clinician oversight beyond his own practice was mentioned, and no clearance question was asked.

signals: Self-directed and capable, with a cheap alternative that genuinely worked - eighteen months to two years of self-taught kettlebell training from YouTube producing 'pretty good results' and a spine that feels stronger
Anchored his own ceiling in the first ninety seconds, before any discovery: 'if it's like $2,000, I'm good. If it's like eight or nine, I'm out'
Explicitly refused the discovery process: 'we could probably mainstream this a little bit more. You don't have to know all my emotional stuff'
Declined on value rather than money and said so directly: 'I can afford it. But just because I can afford it doesn't mean I should'
Price-literate on both sides of the table - he sells $10,000 packages himself and reasons explicitly about value-to-price ratios
Not the_optimizer despite the profile fitting: price was a hard barrier here, not a quality signal

goals.text: Level up his kettlebell technique so he stops injuring himself as he increases the weight
Keep his body functional and healthy so he can carry on doing all of this for the next twenty or thirty years without giving anything up to being old and broken
Build out his upper body and thighs - he considers himself strong but not twenty-something strong
Reduce body fat and get his abs to show again, which he believes is mostly a nutrition problem
Get proper education on technique, since he is entirely self-taught from YouTube
Pass safe technique on to his wife and two young children so they do not damage their backs
Heal from his existing injuries rather than manage around them

pains.text: Two disc herniations at L5-S1 and L4-L5 from a car accident, plus a microdiscectomy, with flare-ups whenever he trained at high intensity in the old style
Unsolidified kettlebell technique - either overdoing the weight or not having the movement right, with injury as the consequence
Reverts to ego lifting despite knowing better, which he says is murder on his shoulders and back
Asynchronous video form feedback was too slow and too much hassle to be worth it when he tried it before
Fear that a paid programme would turn out to be no different from the free videos he already watches
At fifty, aware he is no longer as strong as he was and does not want to lose further ground
Body fat he cannot shift without being stricter on nutrition, which he has not done

objections.raw_quote: It's not that I don't value what you guys are doing. I think all this is wonderful material. I think it's good stuff. Um, I did. I don't. yeah. I know that I would value it that high is the only thing. Like $2,000, $3,000, no problem. Where do I sign? So I don't know if you have another version like that
objections.rep_response: Asked one clarifying question - 'Is it just the amount or is it?' - then argued from the size of the task: 'you're 50 years old. talking about potentially undoing 50 years of dysfunctional movement patterns'. Never asked what would make it worth $6,000 to him, and never mentioned Primal University despite the prospect asking outright whether another version existed.

objections.raw_quote: I just think $1,000 a month, you know, even if I found someone here locally to teach me some of these things, I know I wouldn't be paying $1,000 a month to work, you know, to work together that much. That's really the only thing, you know, like, I value it. And I would separate. I would definitely pay in the thousands to do it. I just can't pay $6,000. That's a little much for me.
objections.rep_response: Offered to break up the payment - 'Even if we split it up for you, it's not a...' - and was immediately corrected that affordability was not the issue. Did not pivot to value once the diagnosis was disproved.

objections.raw_quote: My fear, my fear is that I would get in this program and I would be like, this isn't any different than me watching some of these videos.
objections.rep_response: Conceded the uncertainty before answering it - 'I guess you don't really know until you're in it' - then differentiated on feedback: 'the videos don't give you feedback. They're just videos.' Followed with a series of questions about what a local trainer could not do, including 'If you keep doing that, you're going to dislocate something.' No risk reversal, no guarantee, no trial and no proof was offered.

objections.raw_quote: My thing is, I just, you know, I've talked to other people, I've been through this process before, and if it's like $2,000, I'm good. If it's like, joining me. Thanks, Eight or nine, I'm out. So we could probably mainstream this a little bit more. You don't have to know all my emotional stuff. I'm with you. I like it. So I sell high-ticket items. I sell $10,000 decompression packages to people. So I've worked off all that stuff.
objections.rep_response: Accepted the terms completely and abandoned the discovery process for the rest of the call. Never returned to goals, consequences or commitment. Proposed label: prospect_refuses_discovery_and_pre_anchors_price.

offer.payment_plan_terms: Raised only as an unfinished question - 'Even if we split it up for you, it's not a...' - with no structure, instalment count, deposit or total ever stated. The prospect declined it as irrelevant before any terms were discussed.

evidence: Clear and final refusal: 'the program sounds wonderful, you know, and for a few grand, I would do it, but, uh, five, six, it's probably just a little higher than I need to go'
He pre-declared the disqualifying range before discovery even began: 'if it's like $2,000, I'm good. If it's like eight or nine, I'm out'
Explicitly not an affordability loss - 'I can afford it. But just because I can afford it doesn't mean I should' - so this is a value refusal from a prospect with the money
He stated an alternative plan he intends to pursue instead: recording and self-analysing his own form against free educational videos, and possibly finding someone locally
No payment taken, no link sent, no follow-up scheduled
Counter-evidence: he left the door genuinely open - 'if anything changes, I will reach out' - and had asked directly whether a cheaper version existed, which was never answered
outcome.next_step: None set. Prospect said he would reach out if anything changed. No follow-up date, no material sent, and no Primal University link offered despite him asking whether another version existed.

notable.note: The most commercially significant miss in the batch. A 50-year-old doctor who runs his own practice, sells $10,000 packages himself, said outright 'I can afford it', asked directly 'I don't know if you have another version like that', and stated he would pay a few thousand and would separately pay for the nutrition piece - and was offered nothing. Primal University at $199 a month was never mentioned, despite the same rep leading with it on two other calls in this same batch. Underneath that, the rep let the prospect cancel discovery in the first ninety seconds and never recovered: a man with two disc herniations, a spinal surgery, a stated fear of ending up 'too old and broken', and a five-year-old son and eight-year-old daughter who copy his kettlebell workouts, and not one question was asked about any of it.

quality.notes: Moderate inversion, mostly at turn boundaries where the rep's question is appended to the prospect's turn or vice versa. Clear cases at 00:03:06 ('is like, have you specifically reached out to anyone' runs into the prospect's answer), 00:03:28 and 00:05:51 where the injury exchange crosses labels, and 00:22:57 where 'To send it to Trevor, I'd have to record myself' is attributed to the rep but is the prospect. The prospect's speaker label is the Zoom handle 'dstithem' throughout. Long passages are reliable and role assignment was read from content.
